section_summary: This section contains late-1937 proposals for influencing American views of Japan through newspapers, radio, films, lectures, books, magazines, music, food and educational institutions. It also records a 1938 pamphlet campaign and includes David Warren Ryder’s résumé and supporting references. The final pages shift to a 1947 State Department memorandum and a translated list of payments from Japanese consular secret funds.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of an educational campaign proposal
subfiles.about: The writer concludes an earlier proposal for improving American attitudes toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Advocates indirect educational work to reduce hostility and encourage Americans to consider Japan’s viewpoint.

subfiles.title: Outline of Educational Campaigns, Plans 1–4
subfiles.about: Four annual budgets set out alternative combinations of offices, publications, radio, films, lectures and pamphlets.
subfiles.summary: The plans propose annual spending of roughly $300,000 or $500,000. Each funds a news bureau and newspaper and magazine work; the alternatives vary the scale of radio, motion pictures, lectures and pamphlet distribution. Headquarters would be in San Francisco, with branches in New York City and Chicago.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Accompanying and Explaining Plans Numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4
subfiles.about: Ryder explains how the four proposed educational campaigns would operate.
subfiles.summary: Ryder describes a weekly clip sheet, negotiated newspaper and magazine articles, and radio broadcasts built around cultural subjects to influence opinion indirectly. He also explains industrial films, lecturers and monthly pamphlets. The four plans adjust their scale and mix, including an option without radio.

subfiles.title: Radio, Prize Story, and Newspaper Publicity Proposals
subfiles.about: The writer proposes several forms of American publicity using Japanese cultural material.
subfiles.summary: Proposals include broadcasts from Japan, recorded radio programs, paid talks by scholars, a prize story backed by publishers and film companies, and human-interest stories and photographs for newspaper syndicates. The writer suggests Lee & Perkins could coordinate distribution and subsidies.

subfiles.title: Magazines
subfiles.about: The writer proposes supplying Japanese material to popular and business magazines.
subfiles.summary: Lee & Perkins would translate story ideas and prepare industry articles for American magazines.

subfiles.title: Lecturers
subfiles.about: The writer proposes a paid information service for American lecturers on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lee & Perkins would offer lecturers research, photographs, films and slides at nominal cost.

subfiles.title: Music and Phonograph Records
subfiles.about: The writer proposes adapting Japanese music for American publication and performance.
subfiles.summary: An American arranger would prepare Japanese melodies and English lyrics for sheet music, radio, films and records. The writer also suggests prize competitions and estimates first-year expenses at $35,000.

subfiles.title: Japan Gazette: Distribution in America
subfiles.about: The writer outlines pricing, subscriptions and newsstand distribution for Japanese magazines in America.
subfiles.summary: The proposal targets libraries, colleges and newsstands, recommends a lower price, and suggests sample copies and joint subscriptions. Its final page briefly discusses changes to Japan in Pictures.

subfiles.title: Book Publishers
subfiles.about: The writer proposes helping American publishers issue and distribute books favorable to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lee & Perkins would share selected publishing costs, stock English-language books printed in Japan, translate illustrated works, and broker publication rights. The writer argues that these measures would increase American access to authoritative books about Japan.

subfiles.title: Institutions in America Specializing in Japanese or Far Eastern Subjects
subfiles.about: The writer proposes grants to American institutions and a traveling Japanese studies course.
subfiles.summary: Small grants would support publications and lectures. A university-sponsored course would combine study aboard ship with travel and instruction in Japan, potentially beginning in 1938.

subfiles.title: Japanese Food
subfiles.about: The writer proposes promoting Japanese cuisine through American restaurant chains.
subfiles.summary: Lee & Perkins would recruit trade sponsors and send a Japanese chef to introduce dishes such as tempura and sukiyaki.

subfiles.title: Lee & Perkins
subfiles.about: Perkins describes the partnership’s origins, personnel and commercial projects.
subfiles.summary: Perkins recounts his advertising work with Harry Lee and their later effort to market Japanese products, publications and designs in America. He lists current trade projects and explains that both partners still work on the firm part time.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Takahashi: Highlights of Pamphlet Campaign
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports publication, distribution, subscriptions and responses to a pamphlet campaign.
subfiles.summary: Ryder reports large pamphlet and leaflet printings, requests for additional copies, new mailing-list entries, subscriptions, newsstand sales and correspondence. He lists cities reached and describes efforts to answer readers’ questions about Japan and China.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Mr. Takahashi: Annual Subscribers
subfiles.about: The memorandum names annual pamphlet subscribers and reports remaining leaflet stock.
subfiles.summary: Lists 23 subscribers by occupation and notes approximately 8,400 “They Say” leaflets remain.

subfiles.title: Personal Services of D. W. R.
subfiles.about: Ryder lists the work covered by his proposed personal services.
subfiles.summary: Includes writing, printing, mailing, radio addresses, distribution, contact lists and publicity negotiations.

subfiles.title: Outline of Career and Experience of David Warren Ryder
subfiles.about: Ryder summarizes his journalism, publicity and editorial career.
subfiles.summary: The résumé describes Ryder’s earlier Japanese publicity work, his post with the Industrial Association of San Francisco, and his work for American-Hawaiian Steamship Company. It lists publications to which he contributed and identifies supporting references.

subfiles.title: George Harvey’s appraisal of Ryder’s article
subfiles.about: Harvey comments on Ryder’s article about Japanese people and the Pacific Coast.
subfiles.summary: Harvey praises Ryder’s presentation of the California Japanese question as informed and fair, and quotes his argument that Japanese residents need opportunities to become Americans.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing Industrial Association resolutions
subfiles.about: Boynton sends Ryder certified resolutions acknowledging his work.
subfiles.summary: Encloses resolutions and expresses the directors’ appreciation for Ryder’s publicity work.

subfiles.title: Industrial Association resolutions concerning David Warren Ryder
subfiles.about: The board records appreciation for Ryder’s service as publicity director.
subfiles.summary: Accepts Ryder’s resignation with regret and commends four years of publicity work.

subfiles.title: Rough Outline of Proposals Regarding Newspapers, Magazines, Business and Trade Publications
subfiles.about: Ryder proposes placing material favorable to Japan across the American press.
subfiles.summary: Ryder proposes approaching Hearst and Scripps-Howard papers, individual newspapers, Catholic publications, magazines and trade journals. He argues that personal editorial contacts and selected anti-Communist themes could secure wide publication of Japan’s viewpoint.

subfiles.title: Names from Japanese Consulate Secret Service Fund Account Books
subfiles.about: Okami forwards names found in Japanese consular secret-fund records and identifies additional suspected propaganda agents.
subfiles.summary: Okami describes account books covering payments in 1939–1941 and cautions that abbreviated Japanese entries make the purposes difficult to determine. He notes payments to S. W. Burmingham and lists five people found in San Francisco files as apparent Japanese propaganda agents.

subfiles.title: Secret Expense for Investigation of Communists: Name List of Americans
subfiles.about: The extract itemizes 1939 payments from a Japanese consular secret fund.
subfiles.summary: The table records payments to Walsh, Edmonde, Wright, Garren, Matheson and S. W. Burmingham for compensation, travel, information and work connected with the Dies Committee. A closing note explains that Garren’s surname is spelled differently in a second account book.
